post.description:
Provision a new tenant + invite its first user (super_admin).

Mints a fresh ``tenant_id``, creates the ``tenants`` row through the shared
``tenant_provisioning.create_tenant`` (``created_via='super_admin'``), and
invites ``email`` into it with ``workspace_role`` via ``invite_user`` — the
Keycloak identity is found or created by provisioning's identity invite API
(no attributes, no realm role; P2: membership lives in w2v), which also sends
the action email the account needs. Provisioning returns no account state,
so neither does this response. The invitee becomes a member by accepting
the invite. The tenant's licences are TENANT-level — ensured through the
licences ``w2v`` bundle and held by ``svc:<tenant>:<app>``, never by the
invited person; the audit row's subject is the one w2v's own ``tenant_members``
already knows for the email, else none until the invitee logs in and accepts
(w2v reads nothing from Keycloak). A ``pending`` provisioning_audit row is committed first; on
any failure after that it flips to ``partial`` (KC/licenses side effects are
NOT rolled back — an operator inspects the row) and the error surfaces.
Returns the per-app licence tokens ONCE (no password is ever minted).

get.description:
Bounded wrapper: see ``_RUN_DETAIL_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`` above (#949) — a
dead/unreachable Postgres must surface as a fast 503, not a 120s hang.

Lightweight live-status projection for the run-monitor's safety-net poll.

Returns run-level status plus each stage's lifecycle state — and nothing
else. Deliberately omits every stage ``output`` blob, ``config_snapshot``
and ``usage_total`` that ``GET /{run_id}`` (RunDetail) ships: polling that
heavy payload every few seconds grew with each completed stage and froze
the browser on long multi-stage runs. The full detail is fetched once on
terminal for the final render.

``Cache-Control: no-store`` is REQUIRED: this is a high-frequency poll whose
whole purpose is to observe a state transition (running → completed). Without
it, an intermediary HTTP cache (a client's request context, a browser fetch)
can serve a cached pre-completion ``running`` response for the remainder of
the poll even after the run is terminal — the run never *looks* done to the
poller though the DB (and every replica) says ``completed``. This was the
root cause of the e2e website-review shard's ~20-min stale-``running`` hang
(2026-07-03): verified live that all orchestrator pods returned ``completed``
while the poll still saw ``running``.

get.summary: Download the run's soft-CC caption track as an SRT file
get.description:
Mint and return the run's soft-CC captions as a downloadable ``.srt``.

Built on demand from the run's narration timing (the same accurate track the
YouTube publish path attaches), so it's available regardless of whether the
run was ever published — the published-modal link only existed transiently.
Returns 404 for a run with no captionable narration (audiobook / unrecognised)
or when the caller's tenant does not own it.

get.summary: Download an audit run's scorecard as a PDF report
get.description:
Render an audit run's scorecard to a downloadable PDF, on demand.

Built from the run's ``<type>_scan`` structured output (seo_audit / cro_audit /
marketing_scorecard — the same data the frontend scorecard renders) → a
self-contained HTML page →
html_render_service's headless-Chromium print. On demand (no stored artifact) so
it's always current and adds no render cost to a run that is never downloaded.
404 for a run the caller's tenant doesn't own or that has no audit scorecard.

post.description:
Create a child run that reuses what is still valid and re-runs the rest.

``from_stage`` given — the "rerun this stage" action: re-run that stage and
everything depending on it, reuse every other completed stage. 422 if it is not
a stage of this run's blueprint.

No ``from_stage`` (the Studio's Restart / regenerate) on a failed, cancelled or
completed parent: a per-stage plan (``services/runs/restart_plan.py``, previewed
by ``GET /runs/{id}/restart-plan``) re-runs the stages that did not finish, have
open feedback, read a run input that changed, or depend on a stage the user
edited — and reuses everything else. Where the plan cannot reuse anything (or the
blueprint cannot resume safely) the legacy annotation-driven partition applies:
cut at the stages with open feedback, else re-run everything.

get.description:
Preview what ``POST /runs/{id}/regenerate {}`` would reuse and re-run.

Read-only. 409 for a run that is still active (``pending``/``running``) or
``paused`` (a paused run is resumed in place, not restarted). The answer is
computed from the CURRENT project state, so it moves when the user edits.

post.description:
Rearrange the clip timeline and re-stitch the video as a new version.

Spawns a child run that preserves every stage before the blueprint's compile
cut (with ``stage_name``'s clip array reordered to ``ordered_element_ids``)
and re-runs only the compile stage onward — reusing every generated clip
asset. Returns the child ``RunSummary`` so the UI navigates to the new
version (its lineage shows on ``GET /runs/{id}/ancestors``).

422 if the stage is not a clip spine, the blueprint has no compile stage
downstream, or the parent run is not completed (only a finished timeline can
be re-stitched); 400 if ``ordered_element_ids`` is not a permutation of the
stage's ids; 409 if the parent run is still running.

Apply per-clip edits (trim / anchor / caption / fit) and/or a music-bed
change; re-stitch the video as a version.

Spawns a child run that preserves every stage before the blueprint's compile
cut — with ``stage_name``'s clip array carrying each edited clip's override
fields — and re-runs only the compile stage onward, reusing every generated
clip asset. Per-clip edits live on the spine stage output (survive down the
run lineage); a run-level ``music`` change is merged into the run's
``sound_effects`` config and passed as a config override (never mutates the
project brief). Returns the child ``RunSummary`` so the UI navigates to the
new version.

**A pipeline whose CUT is timed to the bed rewinds further.** ``action_reel``
snaps every shot boundary to the selected track's beat grid, so re-stitching a
new bed over the old cut would ship a reel cut to a track it does not play. For
those blueprints the music change instead re-runs from ``music_select`` (see
``runs/elements.music_rewind_stage``) so the grid and the cut are re-derived,
the footage branch is preserved, and the choice rides the ``music`` config block
the stage actually reads — NOT ``sound_effects``, which no ``action_reel`` stage
reads. Such a request must carry no per-clip ``edits`` (that pipeline has no
clip spine) → 422.

Same completed-only gate as reorder (only a finished timeline can be
re-stitched): 422 if the stage is not a clip spine, the blueprint has no
compile stage downstream, or the parent run is not completed; 400 if none of
the edited clip ids exist on the current timeline; 409 if the parent run is
still running.

Re-narrate a single line (new text and/or voice) and re-stitch as a version.

Spawns a child run that re-synthesizes EXACTLY ONE TTS clip — the addressed
line's — patches that line's text on the stage the narrate handler reads (so the
captions match the new audio) plus that one clip entry on the narrate stage's
preserved output, and re-runs only the compile stage onward. Every sibling
clip's audio is reused byte-identically. Returns the child ``RunSummary``.

Same completed-only gate as apply-edits / reorder (only a finished timeline can
be re-stitched): 422 if the stage is not a clip spine, the parent run is not
completed, the pipeline has no narration stage between the spine and the compile
cut, the clip cannot be resolved to a source line, or the clip already carries an
UPLOADED voiceover (which would win over the TTS in ``assemble_shots``, making the
re-narrate silently inaudible — remove it first). 409 if the parent is running.

Regenerate a single clip's image and re-stitch as a new version.

Spawns a child run that preserves the spine (and every sibling clip's assets)
verbatim and re-runs only the per-clip image stage onward, folding this clip's
open feedback into just its prompt — so exactly one image regenerates while
every other clip is reused. Returns the child ``RunSummary``.

422 if the stage is not a clip spine, the parent run is not completed (its
sibling clips must already exist to be reused), or the pipeline cannot target
a single clip surgically (no per-clip image stage, static round-robin
prompts, no line_id, or no open feedback on the clip) — the UI then falls
back to the annotation-driven ``regenerate``. 409 if the parent run is still
running.

patch.description:
Shallow-merge `body.patch` into one element inside StageOutput.output.

Element addressing reuses `_ELEMENT_PATHS` from `services/runs/elements.py`.
The element's `id` is preserved regardless of `patch` content. The read takes
a row lock (`get_for_update`) so a concurrent edit of a DIFFERENT element in
the same stage output is not silently discarded.

Allowed on every run the executor does not own — paused, completed, failed and
CANCELLED (409 on pending/running). Nothing downstream changes in place; the edit
stamps ``edited_at``, so a later Restart / regenerate keeps this stage's edited
output and re-runs only the stages depending on it (``restart_plan.py``).

Override chapter titles and sub-chapter visibility on a course's
``course_stitch`` output.

Overrides are keyed by the chapter's stable ``chapter_key`` (see
``_chapter_key``): the bare ``lesson_project_id`` for a per-lesson (level-0)
marker, ``f"{lesson_project_id}#{ordinal}"`` for a per-slide (level-1)
sub-chapter — both stable across re-stitches, unlike sequence or the slide's
fresh uuid. They are stored as the source of truth in
``chapter_title_overrides`` and ALSO folded into ``chapters[].title`` in
place (a denormalized copy so any consumer reading raw chapters sees the
edit). Unknown chapter key → 404.

``hidden`` (None = leave untouched, full-replacement otherwise) is the set of
level-1 ``chapter_key``\ s to drop from the published YouTube chapters + the
in-app player; it is stored in ``hidden_chapter_keys`` and denormalized as a
``chapters[].hidden`` bool. Only level-1 sub-chapters are hideable — a lesson
(level-0) or unknown key → 404.

Override (or clear) the course video thumbnail / poster.

A non-null ``thumbnail_url`` must be an artifact URL the orchestrator owns
(validated by ``_is_presignable_artifact_url``) — it is stored as
``thumbnail_override_url`` and preferred over the auto AI cover by both the
in-app poster and the YouTube passthrough. ``null`` clears the override and
reverts to the auto cover (``thumbnail_url`` is left untouched throughout, so
the revert is lossless).

post.description:
Replace one element's value (id preserved) and reset downstream stages.

Unlike `runs.stages.elements.patch` (shallow-merge, downstream untouched in
place), a restamp:

1. Fully replaces the addressed element with ``body.value`` (the element's
   ``id`` is preserved regardless of ``value`` content).
2. Sets every downstream stage_output (per the run's blueprint topological
   order) to ``status='pending'`` with ``output=null`` and ``error=null``.

After a restamp the caller is expected to ``POST /runs/{id}/regenerate``
to re-execute the reset stages (the restart plan re-runs them and reuses the
rest). The restamp itself does NOT spawn a new run — same run-id, same
stage_output row, fresh content. 409 on a pending/running run (the executor owns
the rows) and on a completed one (it would destroy the delivered output).

post.description:
Queue an AI image for this panel; poll or watch the project SSE channel.

202, not 200: an image is minutes of GPU work, far past any request budget.
The panel's ``media_ref`` + ``gen`` are the durable result; the returned job
is TTL-bounded progress. Progress also lands on ``projects:{project_id}``,
the channel ``GET /api/projects/{id}/events`` already streams — storyboard
rows carry no ``run_id``, so there is no run channel to use.

get.summary: Stream this panel's generated image from in-cluster MinIO
get.description:
Serve the panel's own image to the browser.

``media_ref.url`` points at ``minio.internal``, which does not resolve outside
the cluster, so the SPA is handed this path instead (see
``api/panel_image_url``). The bytes are read with the orchestrator's own MinIO
credentials, which carry no expiry — unlike the stored 1h presigned signature.

There is deliberately **no** caller-supplied bucket or key — but resolving the
panel is NOT on its own enough to authorise the object. ``media_ref`` is
client-writable, so a caller can point its own panel at a stranger's key;
authorising only the panel would make this a confused deputy, since MinIO is
read with the orchestrator's credentials. ``panel_object_ref`` therefore also
confines the key to a prefix derived from the panel's ``project_id`` and the
authenticated tenant. Both gates are required; neither is sufficient.

404 (not 403) for a panel of another tenant — the repository is tenant-scoped
and a cross-tenant panel simply does not resolve, matching every sibling panel
route. A panel with no usable image, and a panel whose ref points somewhere it
does not own, are the same 404: the caller learns nothing from the difference.

The ``Content-Type`` is derived from the object KEY rather than forwarded from
MinIO's stored metadata. Every stage artifact written before
``storage_service.guess_artifact_content_type`` existed carries
``application/json`` in its metadata whatever it actually is, and those objects
are not being re-written — so a browser gets the type from the extension the
writer chose (``…/{media_id}.png``), which is the panel's own record of the
format. Forwarding the stored value would keep serving PNGs as JSON.

Poll one panel-image job.

Tenancy is re-checked against the PANEL (the database), never against the
job record — the record lives in Redis under a guessable-shaped id and is
not an authorization artifact. A job whose ``panel_id`` does not match the
path is a 404 for the same reason.

``media_ref.url`` is rewritten to the panel's image-proxy path on the way out
(``api/panel_image_url``); the stored ``minio.internal`` URL would not load in
a browser.

delete.description:
Delete a MANUAL snapshot. ``auto`` snapshots are machine-managed (minted by
restore, capped by retention) — deleting one by hand would punch a hole in the
undo trail, so they are 409, not 204. ``branch_base`` is machine-managed the same
way (minted by fork, it IS the base side of the branch's three-way merge diff):
hand-deleting one would CASCADE the branch row away and silently strand the fork,
so it is 409 too — the only sanctioned way to remove it is to delete the branch.

post.description:
Roll the board back to a snapshot. ``expected_lock_versions`` is REQUIRED — this is
the sharpest write in the storyboard (it rewrites scenes + panels + assets wholesale),
so an unguarded restore discards a sibling's work with no trace. 400 without the map,
409 when the live board no longer matches it.

Fork the project's storyboard into a hidden child project (201).

``project_id`` may itself be a BRANCH — that used to be a blanket 409 and is now
supported. The fork is 1-hop whatever it forks: the link row points at ``project_id``,
so the new branch's "root" is its IMMEDIATE parent and diff/merge/lock/RLS need no
special case. The rule that keeps a chain sound is on the way back UP, not here — a
branch with open children of its own refuses to merge or abandon (409), which forces
the chain to close bottom-up instead of stranding the children in a parent that has
already gone terminal. See ``OpenChildBranchesError``.

get.description:
One bounded, newest-first page of the root's branches. ``status`` is optional and
means NO filter when omitted — which is NOT the same as "the open ones".

delete.description:
Close a branch WITHOUT merging it and archive its child project (204).

DELETE is the verb, but this is an ABANDON, not a destroy: the child project is
archived, because its panels are the only record of the discarded work.

A ``merged`` branch is 409, not a silent no-op: ``merged`` is terminal, the root
already holds its content, and the merge already archived the child — so abandoning it
would be a pointless re-archive of the very project the merge's provenance still points
at. Re-abandoning an already-``abandoned`` branch is idempotent (204) — only ``merged``
conflicts.

409.description: branch already merged, or it has open child branches

get.description:
Three-way diff: ``base`` (the fork's pinned ``branch_base`` snapshot) vs ``main``
(the root's board NOW) vs ``branch`` (the child's board NOW).

Entries are keyed by LINEAGE (``origin_id or id``), never by panel id — ids are
re-minted per project, so an id-keyed diff would be pure noise.

Readable for a CLOSED branch too (that is how you audit what a merge did); only
APPLYING a closed branch is refused.

``root_fingerprint`` is the optimistic-concurrency token: hand it back to the merge,
which 409s if the root moved in between. It is a content hash of the root's whole
board (panels + scenes + assets), not a timestamp — a clock etag skews across the
orchestrator's replicas and would fire on writes that changed nothing.

post.description:
Apply the branch onto the root, then close it as ``merged``.

``root_fingerprint`` (from the diff) is REQUIRED and is the concurrency contract: if
the root moved since the caller read the diff, this is a 409 rather than a silent
clobber of whatever landed on main while the human was deciding.

``resolutions`` need only cover what the caller overrides — a non-conflict entry
defaults to ``branch`` (merging the branch is what was asked for). A ``conflict`` has
NO default: merging one unresolved is a 422, not a coin-flip, because picking a side
is the decision the human opened the diff to make.

409 also covers a ``merged``/``abandoned`` branch: both are terminal. Re-merging would
replay stale content onto a root that has moved on; merging an abandoned branch would
resurrect work its author explicitly discarded.

The HTTP replacement for the in-pod ``host_package.py`` script: an authored
recording bundle becomes a ``brief.package_url`` over plain multipart, so
neither an agent nor the frontend needs pod access to drive a showcase run.

post.summary: Stage a per-clip voiceover replacing one shot's TTS narration.
post.description:
Stage an uploaded narration take and return its URL + probed duration.

Tenant-scoped like the thumbnail upload (the upload precedes the clip-edit
PATCH that references it). The returned ``audio_url`` goes onto a ``ClipEdit``
as the shot's ``audio_url`` — it REPLACES that shot's TTS narration — and
``seconds`` becomes its ``audio_seconds``, which declares the shot's length
(the compiler ffprobes the audio and freeze-pads the visual to it, so the FE
must show the caller how far the clip will stretch).

The duration is probed HERE, server-side: an unprobeable file is a 400 and is
never stored, because the compiler resolves an unfetchable/undecodable
``audio_url`` to SILENCE without failing the render.

The take is then LOUDNESS-NORMALIZED to -18 LUFS / -1.5 dBTP — the exact level
``tts_backend`` masters every synthesized clip to — before it is stored. The
compiler applies no gain to ``shot.audio_url``, so storing an operator's raw
take (a phone recording at -30 LUFS, a hot bounce at -8) next to pre-mastered
TTS neighbours is a 10-20 dB level jump mid-video. See
``src.services.audio_premaster``; it fails open, so a premaster that can't run
degrades to today's un-normalized behaviour and never fails the upload.

**Probe ordering:** the ORIGINAL bytes are probed first (that probe is the
decodability gate whose 400 must not change), premastering runs second, and
the NORMALIZED bytes are re-probed third — because a re-encode can shift the
duration by a frame (encoder priming/padding on mp3/aac) and ``seconds`` must
describe the artifact that is actually stored, which is what the compiler
freeze-pads the visual to. If the re-probe can't read the normalized output,
that is treated as one more fail-open path: the ORIGINAL bytes and their
probed duration are stored.

Stage a reference image for a project's Asset library and return its URL.

Tenant-scoped like the thumbnail and voiceover uploads: the upload precedes
the ``POST /api/projects/{id}/storyboard/assets`` (or the PATCH) that
references it, so it cannot be project-scoped. The returned ``image_url``
is what the caller appends to the asset's ``reference_images`` — that list is
a ``list[str]`` of fetchable URLs, and until this route existed there was no
way for a client to produce one.

The bytes are magic-byte validated (``_image_format``) before anything is
written: the extension and the multipart content-type are both
attacker-controlled, and this bucket is readable back through the artifact
proxy, so a renamed script must never land in it.

post.summary: Upload one raw source clip (.mp4/.mov/.m4v) for an action_reel project.
post.description:
Stream ONE source clip to storage and register it as a ``video_sources`` row.

One file per request by design: a multi-file part would either serialise the
uploads behind one HTTP request (no browser progress per clip, one failure
kills the batch) or force the whole set through this worker at once. Ten
parallel single-clip POSTs is what the FE actually wants.

Validation runs cheapest-and-most-decisive first, so a doomed upload dies
before its body is drained:

1. extension + ``video/*`` content-type → 415 (zero bytes read);
2. a declared ``Content-Length`` already over the cap → 413 (zero bytes read
   — this is what stops a 4 GB body from being streamed to disk only to be
   rejected at the end);
3. magic bytes on the FIRST chunk → 400 (nothing stored);
4. the running byte total → 413, aborting mid-stream;
5. an empty body → 400.

get.summary: List a project's uploaded source clips.
get.description:
List the project's source clips, oldest first (upload order = shoot order).

Each row carries a freshly presigned ``original_url``: the presign TTL is an
hour, so URLs must be minted per read rather than stored on the row.

delete.summary: Remove an uploaded source clip from a project.
delete.description:
Delete the row; sweep the objects best-effort.

The ROW is the record of truth the FE and the cut stage read, so its removal
is what the caller is promised. The bucket sweep (original + every derived
preview/poster/sprite under the same key tree) is deliberately fail-open:
MinIO being unreachable must not leave the operator unable to remove a clip
they uploaded by mistake, and a stranded object is bucket-lifecycle garbage
that no one can address anyway once the row is gone.

post.summary: Begin a chunked upload of one source clip (for files over the edge body limit).
post.description:
Reserve an upload and hand back the slicing plan. ZERO bytes are read.

Every reject a doomed upload can earn is earned HERE, on a JSON body of a few
hundred bytes, before the client spends ten minutes pushing 500 MiB up a
domestic uplink:

1. extension not in the allowlist → 415;
2. content type not ``video/*`` → 415;
3. declared size over ``_VIDEO_MAX_BYTES`` → 413.

The magic-byte gate cannot run here — no bytes exist yet — so it runs on the
first chunk of part 1, which is the earliest moment a container head can be
judged. That is the same guarantee the single-shot route gives, just deferred
by one request.

``source_id`` is pre-allocated so the FINAL key is fixed now. The alternative
(mint the id at ``complete``) would make the part keys unrelated to the final
object, which in turn makes an interrupted ``complete`` unrecoverable: nothing
would tie the orphaned staging tree to the row that should have owned it.

put.summary: Upload one part of a chunked video upload (raw application/octet-stream body).
put.description:
Stream ONE raw part to its staging key and record its size.

The body is ``application/octet-stream``, NOT multipart. That is deliberate:
multipart would add a base64-ish envelope and a boundary scan to every part
for no benefit (there is exactly one field), and the envelope inflates the
body — pushing a 32 MiB part closer to the edge limit this whole surface
exists to stay under. It is drained through ``_drain_to_path`` in 1 MiB
chunks like everything else here; ``await request.body()`` is as forbidden on
this path as ``await file.read()`` is on the other.

**Idempotent.** The key is derived from ``part_number`` alone, so a retried
part overwrites its own object and re-records the same size. There is no
"part already uploaded" error to get stuck behind, which matters because the
common failure this surface exists to survive is a part dying mid-flight.

Three caps, in the order they can fire:

* a declared ``Content-Length`` already over the per-part allowance → 413
  with zero bytes read;
* the running per-part total → 413 mid-stream (so a lying Content-Length
  cannot write more than one part's worth to the pod's disk);
* the running WHOLE-UPLOAD total across every stored part → 413, and because
  that upload can now never succeed, it is ABORTED and its staging tree swept
  in the same breath. The distinction is deliberate: an oversized single part
  is a client bug the client can fix by re-slicing, while an oversized total
  is a file that was never going to fit and whose remaining parts must not be
  allowed to keep filling the bucket.

post.summary: Compose the uploaded parts into one source clip and register it.
post.description:
Compose the parts, measure the result, and register the ``video_sources`` row.

Answers with the BYTE-IDENTICAL ``VideoSourceResponse`` (and 201) that the
single-shot route returns. That is a contract, not a nicety: the frontend has
one upload-completed handler and one generated type, and a chunked upload that
answered with its own shape would fork both — the whole point is that the two
surfaces differ in transport and in nothing else.

Order of operations, each step justified by what it prevents:

1. ``SELECT … FOR UPDATE`` on the upload row — the single-winner fence, see
   below;
2. COMPLETENESS check over parts ``1..part_count`` → 400, and ``sum(parts)``
   against ``bytes_declared`` → 400. A gap means the composed object would be a
   clip with a hole punched in it that still plays for its first few seconds;
   a short tail means the same thing with the hole at the end. Both are the
   worst possible outcome, because nothing downstream would flag either — see
   "why the declared size is enforced" below;
3. if the final object ALREADY EXISTS, skip the compose. A previous attempt
   composed it and then died before its row was durable (see "crash-safety");
4. otherwise compose in ASCENDING part order into the final key. Ordering is
   the entire correctness of the composition: parts are opaque byte ranges,
   and any other order produces a file whose ``moov`` no longer describes its
   ``mdat``;
5. pull the composed object back to a LOCAL file and ``_probe_video`` it;
6. INSERT the row + flip the status, ``commit`` — and only THEN sweep the
   staging tree.

**Crash-safety: the parts are swept AFTER the commit, never before.** They
used to be swept first, which opened a window — a SIGTERM (routine: the
deployment rolls with ``maxSurge: 1``) or any commit failure between the sweep
and the commit rolled the row back with the parts already deleted. The upload
row was still ``open``, so the client retried, the completeness check still
passed against the ledger, and the compose then failed forever because its
sources no longer existed: a permanent 500 on footage that was in fact safely
composed, plus an orphaned object under ``object_key`` with no row pointing at
it. The asymmetry is the whole argument: a leftover part set is recoverable
garbage under a prefix nobody reads, while a missing one is unrecoverable. So
the sweep is the LAST thing this handler does, and step 3 makes the retry that
reaches it converge rather than recompose.

**Why the declared size is enforced.** ``part_count`` and ``bytes_declared``
both come from the browser, and it is tempting to treat them as untrusted
hints (this handler used to check only that the parts it happened to have were
contiguous from 1, never how many there should have been). That is what let 4
of 16 parts compose into a 128 MiB fragment and register as a success. The
count check alone still leaves the tail: 16 of 16 parts where the last one was
truncated mid-flight is the same silent, permanently-zeroed clip. The sum is
the only statement of "this is the whole file" anyone ever makes, so it is
enforced, and the cost is understood: a client that lies about its own file's
size cannot complete. That is the correct outcome — the alternative is
registering a truncated clip as whole.

**Exactly one winner across replicas.** Two ``complete`` calls racing (a
double-click, a retry after a slow first attempt, two browser tabs) hit the
same row: the first takes the lock and holds it to COMMIT, the second blocks,
and — because the lock release re-reads the row under READ COMMITTED — the
second then observes ``status='completed'`` and returns the winner's row
instead of composing again. Without the lock both would INSERT a
``video_sources`` row for the same pre-allocated ``source_id`` and the loser
would surface a duplicate-key 500 on a clip that uploaded perfectly.

**Why the probe pulls the WHOLE object back and not a byte range.** An MP4's
``moov`` atom may sit at the END of the file (anything not written with
``+faststart``, which includes most camera output), so ffprobe needs a
genuinely seekable local copy. A header-only range fetch does not fail loudly:
ffprobe returns nothing usable, ``_probe_video`` degrades to ``{}`` as it is
designed to, and ``footage_probe`` — which never re-probes — permanently
reports zero duration and zero fps for that clip. A silent, permanent loss of
the measurement is far more expensive than one streamed download.

delete.summary: Abandon a chunked upload and discard its staged parts.
delete.description:
Discard an in-flight upload: sweep the staging tree, flip to ``aborted``.

The browser calls this when the user cancels, and it is the only thing that
reclaims the staged parts promptly (nothing else reaps them — see
``_UPLOAD_TTL``). Idempotent by design: aborting an already-aborted upload is
a 204, because a cancel that can fail is a cancel the UI has to explain.

An already-COMPLETED upload keeps its status. Flipping it would contradict the
``video_sources`` row that exists and make ``complete`` recomposable — the way
to remove a finished clip is ``DELETE /video-sources/{source_id}``, which
sweeps the real object tree. The staging sweep still runs (it is a no-op on a
completed upload, and free insurance if the completing pod died before its
own sweep).

post.description:
Publish a completed run's final video to YouTube.

Resolves the run (tenant-scoped), finds its final video artifact, mints a
fresh presigned MinIO URL for it, and starts an upload job on
``youtube_upload_service``. Returns the downstream ``UploadJobResponse``,
echoing the minted ``caption_source`` URL when a soft-CC track was produced
(the upload service's own response doesn't carry it) so the run view can
offer the ``.srt`` as a download.

get.description:
Poll a YouTube upload job (proxied to youtube_upload_service).

Pass the upstream 404 through as a 404 rather than letting the client's
``raise_for_status`` bubble an ``httpx.HTTPStatusError`` into a 500 — a
poller hammering an unreadable job otherwise spams 500s (observed live,
~4/min) and reads as an outage to the caller.

A 404 does NOT mean the job was pruned or expired: ``upload_jobs`` has no
TTL and no prune anywhere in youtube_upload_service. A tenant mismatch is
ONE cause — measured 2026-08-20 on 35 of 48 prod rows (NULL for every row
predating migration ``005_add_owner_tenant_id``, else a sentinel/service
tenant) — but it is NOT the only one, and reading it as the only one costs
a session. Measured 2026-08-23 on the id that produces every one of these
warnings today: upstream's own log reports the owner tenant and the channel
tenant as IDENTICAL. The row simply does not exist. So a 404 here means
"no such job for you", and the caller's next question is whether the id was
ever issued, not only whether the tenants line up.

Hence the ``log.warning`` below: this branch was previously silent at every
level, which is why 484 of these went undiagnosed. Keep it at warning.
Volume is not evidence of breadth — the entire live signal (~90 req/hr,
the service's #2 signature) is ONE external poller re-asking for a single
uuid7 id stamped 2026-06-21 that upstream has never had. No product path
reaches this route: the frontend's ``getUploadJob`` wrapper has no callers.

Every OTHER status now goes through ``_upstream_http_error`` (the ONE upstream
policy) instead of falling out as a raw ``httpx.HTTPStatusError`` -> 500. The 404
branch stays FIRST and unchanged: it is a domain answer this route owns, and
``classify`` would call it permanent and hand back a 502.

post.description:
Retract a published upload: set its YouTube video to private (proxied).

Reduce-only and reversible — youtube_upload_service never raises visibility on
this path, and the video stays on the channel. Scoped to the calling tenant
exactly like the job poll. 404 (no such job for you) and 409 (the job never
published a video) are domain answers passed through; every other upstream
status goes through the ONE upstream policy (``_upstream_http_error``).

Release a private upload: raise its YouTube video to unlisted/public (proxied).

The governed counterpart of :func:`retract_upload_job`, called by marketing's
``marketing.publish_video`` release after a human approved the video. Only
``unlisted``/``public`` are accepted (lowering is /retract). Scoped to the calling
tenant exactly like the job poll; 404/409 are domain answers passed through and
every other upstream status goes through ``_upstream_http_error``.

``tenant_id`` is forwarded EXPLICITLY as the owner scope; it used to be
unaccessed here, so the declared dependency was decorative and the scoping

minted server-side; the user is INVITED into it with ``workspace_role`` (P2:

AdminTenantUpdate.description:

optional but the route rejects an all-None body (nothing to change).

AdminUsageBySlot.description:
Usage per provider slot (P6 ORCH-3).

``slot`` is the tenant connection's slot for in-process (``tenant_byo``) calls,

AdminUsageDetail.title: AdminUsageDetail
AdminUsageDetail.description:

breakdowns by project type, usage stage, and model/provider, and a
cost/token time-series. All figures reflect the requested ``window_days``
(all-time when omitted).

AdminUsagePoint.title: AdminUsagePoint
AdminUsagePoint.description:

``bucket`` is the bucket-start date (the day itself / the Monday for a week /
the 1st for a month). The series is gap-filled — zero-cost buckets appear
between the range ends — and optionally windowed to the last N days.

ApiKeyCreated.title: ApiKeyCreated

ApiKeySummary.title: ApiKeySummary
ApiKeySummary.description: A key as listed — NEVER the secret or its hash; ``prefix`` is public.

ApplyClipEdits.title: ApplyClipEdits

``stage_name`` is the run's clip-spine stage (the storyboard / gen stage whose
output holds the clip array). ``edits`` maps each edited clip's element id →
the fields to override (may be empty for a music-only change). ``music`` is an

(spine edited) and re-runs only the compile stage onward, reusing all generated
